findings.title: Backup code check-and-invalidate is not atomic, allowing reuse via race condition
findings.body: In the credentials authorize() callback, a backup code is validated by decrypting the stored backupCodes array, finding the matching index, then issuing a separate prisma.user.update() to persist the code as used (lines ~137-156). Between the read and the write there is no transaction/lock, so two concurrent login attempts using the same backup code can both pass the `indexOf` check before either write completes, letting a single-use backup code be consumed more than once. Since backup codes are meant to grant exactly one use (per the UI copy 'Each backup code can be used exactly once'), this undermines the single-use guarantee and is a legitimate security/data-integrity issue for a security-sensitive code path.

findings.title: Backup code comparison is case sensitive while generated codes are lowercase hex
findings.body: `backupCodes.indexOf(credentials.backupCode.replaceAll("-", ""))` compares the raw user input against stored codes without normalizing case. Codes are generated with `crypto.randomBytes(5).toString('hex')` which is always lowercase, but the BackupCode input field has no autoCapitalize/autoCorrect restrictions, so mobile keyboards or manual re-typing from a printed copy can introduce uppercase characters, causing a valid backup code to be rejected as incorrect. The same issue exists in `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/disable.ts` line 61.

findings.title: Backup codes are stored with reversible symmetric encryption instead of one-way hashing
findings.body: In `apps/web/pages/api/auth/two-factor/totp/setup.ts` line 68, backup codes are stored using `symmetricEncrypt`, the same reversible scheme used for the TOTP secret. Unlike the TOTP secret (which must be decrypted to compute codes), backup codes only need equality comparison and should be hashed (e.g. bcrypt/sha256) so that leaking CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY does not also reveal every user's plaintext backup codes. Storing them reversibly increases the blast radius of a key compromise.

findings.title: BackupCode component function is misnamed "TwoFactor"
findings.body: The exported default function in BackupCode.tsx is declared as `function TwoFactor({ center = true })`, apparently copy-pasted from TwoFactor.tsx and never renamed. This doesn't break runtime behavior since it's a default export, but it causes React DevTools/profiler and stack traces to show the wrong component name (identical to the actual TwoFactor component), making debugging and future maintenance confusing.

findings.title: No e2e test actually exercises logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code
findings.body: The PR's stated purpose includes 'enable their use during 2fa login flow', but the only backup-code-related additions to the e2e suite are clicking the download/copy/close buttons on the backup codes screen during setup (lines 110-125). There is no test that logs in using a backup code, no test that disables 2FA via the new 'Lost access' backup-code path, and no test for the IncorrectBackupCode/MissingBackupCodes error paths. This gap is explicitly acknowledged by the added comment '// TODO: add more backup code tests, e.g. login + disabling 2fa with backup' but is never addressed, leaving the core new functionality (backup code login, which has the race-condition and case-sensitivity issues noted elsewhere) completely untested.

findings.title: Backup code recovery is unreachable for SSO/magic-link forced-TOTP login flow
findings.body: When a user is routed to the login page via `loginWithTotp` (SSO/email identity providers requiring 2FA, surfaced via the `totpEmail` prop), the footer renders `ExternalTotpFooter` (lines 135-143), which only offers a 'Cancel' button. The 'Lost access' button that toggles `twoFactorLostAccess` (enabling the BackupCode input) only exists in `TwoFactorFooter`, used when `!totpEmail`. As a result, users signing in through Google/SAML/magic-link flows with 2FA enabled have no UI path to use a backup code if they lose access to their authenticator, even though the backend `authorize()` callback supports a `backupCode` credential for exactly this scenario. These users are locked out despite the feature nominally covering the login flow.

findings.title: 2FA is enabled server-side before the UI confirms it, and dismissing the backup-codes screen skips onEnable()
findings.body: After the OTP is verified, `handleEnable` sets `step` to `SetupStep.DisplayBackupCodes` instead of calling `onEnable()` immediately (as it did before this PR). `onEnable()` is now only invoked when the user clicks the explicit 'Close' button (lines 263-272). If the user dismisses the dialog any other way (Escape key, clicking outside, or the dialog's native close affordance via `onOpenChange`), 2FA is already enabled in the database but the parent component is never notified via `onEnable()`, leaving the parent's UI (e.g. the two-factor switch) potentially stale until a manual refresh. Previously this race did not exist because `onEnable()` fired as soon as the server confirmed success.

findings.title: backupCodesUrl Blob object URL is never revoked when the modal is cancelled/closed
findings.body: `setBackupCodesUrl(URL.createObjectURL(textBlob))` (line 99) creates a Blob URL for the downloadable backup codes file. It is only revoked on a subsequent call to `handleSetup` (`if (backupCodesUrl) URL.revokeObjectURL(backupCodesUrl)`, line 98). `resetState()` (lines 71-75), used when the user cancels or closes the modal, does not revoke the URL, so every completed 2FA setup leaks one Blob URL for the lifetime of the page/tab.

findings.title: "missing_backup_codes" message implies a settings action that doesn't exist
findings.body: The string `"missing_backup_codes": "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings."` tells users to regenerate backup codes in settings, but no such explicit 'regenerate backup codes' action was added in this PR — the only way to get new backup codes is to fully disable and re-enable two-factor authentication. The message is misleading and may confuse users trying to find a non-existent settings option.

findings.title: Known-broken test assertion acknowledged via comment but left unfixed
findings.body: A new comment was added: '// FIXME: this passes even when switch is not checked, compare to test below which checks for data-state="checked" and works as expected', directly above `await expect(page.locator('[data-testid=two-factor-switch]').isChecked()).toBeTruthy();` (line 53). The `.isChecked()` call returns a Promise that is never awaited before being wrapped in `expect(...).toBeTruthy()`, so the assertion always passes regardless of actual switch state. The PR author identifies this defect but does not fix it, leaving the first 2FA-enable test unable to actually verify that the switch became checked.
